title: The Need Is Real
author: Phil Hill
summary: This article by education technology analyst Phil Hill steps back from his usual focus on metrics and accountability rules to tell the human story behind vocational training accountability debates: his own daughter, who graduated with a sonography degree and spent eight months filing nearly 200 applications without securing a job. Hill's argument is that the national debate over earnings-premium accountability misses the supply-demand mismatch at the local market level — Phoenix produced so many sonography graduates from multiple programs that employers began requiring two years' experience for entry-level positions, essentially closing the door to new credentials. The piece is a deliberate departure from policy abstraction, acknowledging that Hill has spent most of his writing on what's wrong with accountability rules, but arguing that those critiques can cause us to lose sight of why the concept matters at all: real people trained for real careers and could not get the jobs they were promised. The article is a call for honest analysis that keeps human stakes visible even when arguing about the details of measurement.
points: Supply-demand mismatches at the local market level — not the quality of graduates — can render a perfectly good credential worthless, when multiple programs saturate a regional market faster than employers can absorb new graduates.

When three sonography programs in the same city each graduate a cohort every quarter, employers can require two years of experience for entry-level roles because supply outruns demand — the credential loses its exchange value through market dynamics alone.

The policy debate over earnings-premium accountability can become so focused on measurement flaws that it loses sight of the underlying problem: real people paid for training, completed difficult programs, and cannot get the careers they were promised.
National earnings data and averages obscure the local granularity that matters most — a field can be in-demand nationally while being completely saturated in the city where a program is concentrated.

Honest accountability analysis must keep both dimensions in view: the legitimate critiques of how we measure outcomes and the real human cost when the system fails people who invested years and dollars in credentials that didn't open doors.
quotes: This morning Patrick Methvin of the Gates Foundation made the case for earnings-premium accountability — and acknowledged, as I've argued at length, that the details are hard and the current measures flawed. I haven't changed my mind about any of that. But I've spent most of my words on what's wrong with the rules and too few on something Methvin gets right: the need is real and not just as policy. As a person.

Betsy — my daughter, who does much of the data work behind this newsletter and produces the podcast — graduated last June from a private college in Phoenix with an associate degree in diagnostic medical sonography. By every account an in-demand field, and the program was not easy: twenty-plus hours a week of class, extra lab hours, two years of real work. She finished and then started looking for a job. That was eight months and nearly 200 applications ago. She still doesn't have one.

Phoenix has three sonography programs, two of them graduating a fresh cohort every quarter. All programs in the state of Arizona are concentrated in the city. The local market can't absorb that many new technicians, even if the market is growing overall, so employers have started requiring two years' experience for entry-level roles, because they can.

Supply outruns demand, and the people holding the credential are the ones who pay for the mismatch. Her cohort bears it out: of the dozen who started, only three or four have the jobs they trained for. One moved to Texas to get hers. Betsy has two young kids and can't.

This is the dimension the national earnings debate skips. We argue about whether graduates, in the aggregate, earn more with a credential than without it. We do not argue about what happens when the specific market a program feeds is saturated.
I want to talk about why the concept matters in the first place — because those of us who spend our time scrutinizing the rules can lose sight of the thing the rules are reaching for.
